subsection.title: Introduction
subsection.paragraph: This chapter further explores the power of the derivative as a tool to help analyze the properties of functions. We can use this information to accurately sketch graphs of functions. We also see how the derivative is used in solving a large class of optimization problems, including finding what level of production will yield a maximum profit for a company, finding what level of production will result in minimal cost to a company, finding the maximum height attained by a rocket, finding the maximum velocity at which air is expelled when a person coughs, and a host of other problems.

figure.caption: How many loudspeaker systems should the Acrosonic company produce to maximize its profit? In Example 4, you will see how the techniques of calculus can be used to help answer this question.

subsection.title: Determining the Intervals Where a Function Is Increasing or Decreasing
subsection.paragraph: According to a study by the U.S. Department of Energy and the Shell Development Company, a typical car’s fuel economy as a function of its speed is described by the graph shown in Figure 1. Observe that the fuel economy $$f(x)$$ in miles per gallon (mpg) improves as $$x$$ , the vehicle’s speed in miles per hour (mph), increases from $$0$$ to $$42$$ and then drops as the speed increases beyond $$42$$ mph. We use the terms increasing and decreasing to describe the behavior of a function as we move from left to right along its graph.

figure.caption: A typical car’s fuel economy improves as the speed at which it is driven increases from 0 mph to 42 mph and drops at speeds greater than 42 mph.
figure.alt_text: A curve is graphed in the first quadrant of the coordinate plane with grid lines. The horizontal axis x labeled Speed ranges from 0 to above 80 meters per hour and the vertical axis f (x), labeled Miles per gallon ranges from 0 to above 35. Alongside, a decorative image of a car moving horizontally from left to right is given. The curve starts from the origin, slopes upward to the right, bulges away from the x axis, reaches the highest point at around (40, 33), slopes down to the right, still bulging away from the x axis and ends around (75, 20).
figure.credit: Source: U.S. Department of Energy and Shell Development Co.

subsection.paragraph: More precisely, we have the following definitions:

note.title: Increasing and Decreasing Functions
note.paragraph: A function $$f$$ is increasing on an interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ if for every two numbers $$x_{1}$$ and $$x_{2}$$ in $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ , $$f\left( x_{1} \right) < f\left( x_{2} \right)$$ whenever $$x_{1} < x_{2}$$ (Figure 2a).

A function $$f$$ is decreasing on an interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ if for every two numbers $$x_{1}$$ and $$x_{2}$$ in $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ , $$f\left( x_{1} \right) > f\left( x_{2} \right)$$ whenever $$x_{1} < x_{2}$$ (Figure 2b).

subsection.paragraph: We say that $$f$$ is increasing at a number $$c$$ if there exists an interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ containing $$c$$ such that $$f$$ is increasing on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ . Similarly, we say that $$f$$ is decreasing at a number $$c$$ if there exists an interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ containing $$c$$ such that $$f$$ is decreasing on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ .

Since the rate of change of a function at $$x = c$$ is given by the derivative of the function at that number, the derivative lends itself naturally to being a tool for determining the intervals where a differentiable function is increasing or decreasing. Indeed, as we saw in Chapter 2, the derivative of a function at a number measures both the slope of the tangent line to the graph of the function at the point on the graph of $$f$$ corresponding to that number and the rate of change of the function at that number. In fact, at a number where the derivative is positive, the slope of the tangent line to the graph is positive, and the function is increasing. At a number where the derivative is negative, the slope of the tangent line to the graph is negative, and the function is decreasing (Figure 3).

figure.alt_text: Two graphs a) and b), plot a curve and a line in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. In graph a), the curve begins in the first quadrant above the x axis, slopes upward to the right, and bulging away from the x axis. A tangent line with positive slope, which lies above the curve, begins near the y axis, slopes upward to the right, and touches the curve. From the point of contact, a perpendicular is dropped to the x axis meeting at the mark c. Below the graph, the text f prime c > 0 appears. In graph b), the curve enters at the top of the vertical axis slopes downward to the right, and bulges towards the x axis. A tangent line with negative slope, which lies below the curve, begins near the y axis, slopes downward to the right and touches the curve. From the point of contact, a perpendicular is dropped to the x axis meeting at the mark c. Below the graph, f prime c < 0 is written.

subsection.paragraph: These observations lead to the following important theorem, which we state without proof.

item.paragraph: If $$f^{\prime}(x) > 0$$ for every value of $$x$$ in an interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ , then $$f$$ is increasing on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ .
If $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ for every value of $$x$$ in an interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ , then $$f$$ is decreasing on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ .
If $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ for every value of $$x$$ in an interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ , then $$f$$ is constant on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ .

subsection.paragraph: Recall that the graph of a continuous function cannot have any breaks. As a consequence, a continuous function cannot change sign unless it equals zero for some value of $$x$$ . (See Theorem 5.) This observation suggests the following procedure for determining the sign of the derivative $$f^{\prime}$$ of a function $$f$$ and hence the intervals where the function $$f$$ is increasing and where it is decreasing.

note.title: Determining the Intervals Where a Function Is Increasing or Decreasing

item.paragraph: Find all values of $$x$$ for which $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ or $$f^{\prime}$$ is discontinuous, and identify the open intervals determined by these numbers.
Select a test number $$c$$ in each interval found in step 1, and determine the sign of $$f^{\prime}(c)$$ in that interval.
If $$f^{\prime}(c) > 0$$ , $$f$$ is increasing on that interval.
If $$f^{\prime}(c) < 0$$ , $$f$$ is decreasing on that interval.

problem.paragraph: Find the intervals where the function $$f(x) = x + \frac{1}{x}$$ is increasing and where it is decreasing.

item.paragraph: The derivative of $$f$$ is

Since $$f^{\prime}$$ is not defined at $$x = 0$$ , it is discontinuous there. Furthermore, $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ is equal to zero when $$(x + 1)(x - 1) = 0$$ or $$x = \pm 1$$ . Note that the value of $$f^{\prime}$$ is different from zero in the open intervals $$\left( {- \infty, - 1} \right)$$ , $$\left( {- 1,0} \right)$$ , $$\left( {0,1} \right)$$ , and $$\left( {1,\infty} \right)$$ .

To determine the sign of $$f^{\prime}$$ in each of these intervals, we compute $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ at the test points $$x = - 2, - \frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}{and}2$$ , respectively, obtaining $$f^{\prime}\left( {- 2} \right) = \frac{3}{4}$$ , $$f^{\prime}\left( {- \frac{1}{2}} \right) = - 3$$ , $$f^{\prime}\left( \frac{1}{2} \right) = - 3$$ , and $$f^{\prime}(2) = \frac{3}{4}$$ . From the sign diagram for $$f^{\prime}$$ (Figure 9), we conclude that $$f$$ is increasing on $$\left( {- \infty, - 1} \right)$$ and $$\left( {1,\infty} \right)$$ and decreasing on $$\left( {- 1,0} \right)$$ and $$\left( {0,1} \right)$$ .

subsection.title: Relative Extrema
subsection.paragraph: Besides helping us determine where the graph of a function is increasing and decreasing, the first derivative may be used to help us locate certain “high points” and “low points” on the graph of $$f$$ . Knowing these points is invaluable in sketching the graphs of functions and solving optimization problems. These “high points” and “low points” correspond to the relative (local) maxima and relative minima of a function. They are so called because they are the highest or the lowest points when compared with points nearby.

The graph shown in Figure 11 gives the U.S. budget surplus (deficit) from 1996 $$\left( {t = 0} \right)$$ to 2010 $$\left( {t = 14} \right)$$ . The relative maxima and the relative minima of the function $$f$$ are indicated on the graph.

subsection.paragraph: More generally, we have the following definition:

note.title: Relative Maximum
note.paragraph: A function $$f$$ has a relative maximum at $$x = c$$ if there exists an open interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ containing $$c$$ such that $$f(x) \leq f(c)$$ for all $$x$$ in $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ .

subsection.paragraph: Geometrically, this means that there is some interval containing $$x = c$$ such that no point on the graph of $$f$$ with its $$x$$ -coordinate in that interval can lie above the point $$\left( {c,f(c)} \right)$$ ; that is, $$f(c)$$ is the largest value of $$f(x)$$ in some interval around $$x = c$$ . Figure 12 depicts the graph of a function $$f$$ that has a relative maximum at $$x = x_{1}$$ and another at $$x = x_{3}$$ .

figure.caption: f has a relative maximum at x = x 1 and at x = x 3 .
figure.alt_text: A curve y = f(x) is graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. Four marks are labeled x_1, x_2, x_3 and x_4 on the horizontal axis. The open interval containing the point x_1 is labeled I_1 and the open interval containing the point x_3 is labeled I_3. The curve starts at the bottom left of the first quadrant, a short diagonal distance from the origin, slopes upward to the right, bulges away from the x axis and reaches the high point at (x_1, f(x_1)), then it slopes downward, after it inflects between the points x_1 and x_2, it bulges towards the x axis and reaches a low point. Thereafter, it rises upward to the right, and inflects between x_2 and x_3, then it bulges upward and reaches the highest point (x_3, f(x_3)), then it goes down to the right, bulges towards the x axis and reaches the low point and then slopes upward to the right. Perpendiculars are dropped from the points (x_1, f(x_1)) and (x_3, f(x_3)) to meet the horizontal axis at x_1 and x_3 respectively.

subsection.paragraph: Observe that all the points on the graph of $$f$$ with $$x$$ -coordinates in the interval $$I_{1}$$ containing $$x_{1}$$ (shown in blue) lie on or below the point $$\left( {x_{1},f\left( x_{1} \right)} \right)$$ . This is also true for the point $$\left( {x_{3},f\left( x_{3} \right)} \right)$$ and the interval $$I_{3}$$ . Thus, even though there are points on the graph of $$f$$ that are “higher” than the points $$\left( {x_{1},f\left( x_{1} \right)} \right)$$ and $$\left( {x_{3},f\left( x_{3} \right)} \right)$$ , the latter points are “highest” relative to points in their respective neighborhoods (intervals). Points on the graph of a function $$f$$ that are “highest” and “lowest” with respect to all points in the domain of $$f$$ will be studied in Section 4.4.
The definition of the relative minimum of a function parallels that of the relative maximum of a function.

note.title: Relative Minimum
note.paragraph: A function $$f$$ has a relative minimum at $$x = c$$ if there exists an open interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ containing $$c$$ such that $$f(x) \geq f(c)$$ for all $$x$$ in $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ .

subsection.paragraph: The graph of the function $$f$$ depicted in Figure 12 has a relative minimum at $$x = x_{2}$$ and another at $$x = x_{4}$$ .

subsection.title: Finding the Relative Extrema
subsection.paragraph: We refer to the relative maxima and relative minima of a function as the relative extrema of that function. As a first step in our quest to find the relative extrema of a function, we consider functions that have derivatives at such points. Suppose that $$f$$ is a function that is differentiable on some interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ that contains a number $$c$$ and that $$f$$ has a relative maximum at $$x = c$$ (Figure 13a).

figure.alt_text: Two graphs a) and b) each plot a curve and tangent in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The horizontal axis labeled x has marks a, c, and b in order. In graph a, the curve starts directly above the mark a, with a low point, little away from the horizontal axis, bulging away from the x axis and reaches high point. Then, it goes down to the right, and reaches another low point, and ends directly above the mark b. Three perpendiculars are dropped from the starting point, high point and end point of the curve to meet the x axis at a, c, and b respectively. The horizontal line labeled f prime(c) = 0 is drawn at the high point which runs parallel to the x axis. The line labeled f prime x > 0 is drawn to the left side of the curve where the curve changes from bulging down to bulging up and the tangent line labeled f prime x < 0 is drawn to the right side of the curve where the curve changes from bulging up to bulging down. In graph b, the curve starts near the y axis, directly above the mark a, with a high point, slopes downward to the right, bulges towards the x axis, reaches a low point, it turns and goes up to the right and reaches another high point, and ends directly above the mark b Three perpendiculars are dropped from the starting point, low point and ending point of the curve to meet the x axis at a, c, and b respectively. The horizontal line segment labeled f prime c = 0 is drawn at the low point which runs parallel to the x axis. The tangent line labeled f prime x < 0 is drawn to the left side of the curve, which cuts along the curve and the tangent line labeled f prime x > 0 is drawn to the right side of the curve.

subsection.paragraph: Observe that the slope of the tangent line to the graph of $$f$$ must change from positive to negative as we move across $$x = c$$ from left to right. Therefore, the tangent line to the graph of $$f$$ at the point $$\left( {c,f(c)} \right)$$ must be horizontal; that is, $$f^{\prime}(c) = 0$$ (Figure 13a).

Using a similar argument, it may be shown that the derivative $$f^{\prime}$$ of a differentiable function $$f$$ must also be equal to zero at $$x = c$$ if $$f$$ has a relative minimum at $$x = c$$ (Figure 13b).
This analysis reveals an important characteristic of the relative extrema of a differentiable function $$f$$ : At any number $$c$$ where $$f$$ has a relative extremum, $$f^{\prime}(c) = 0$$ .

Before we develop a procedure for finding such numbers, a few words of caution are in order. First, this result tells us that if a differentiable function $$f$$ has a relative extremum at a number $$x = c$$ , then $$f^{\prime}(c) = 0$$ . The converse of this statement—if $$f^{\prime}(c) = 0$$ at $$x = c$$ , then $$f$$ must have a relative extremum at that number—is not true. Consider, for example, the function $$f(x) = x^{3}$$ . Here, $$f^{\prime}(x) = 3x^{2}$$ , so $$f^{\prime}(0) = 0$$ . However, $$f$$ has neither a relative maximum nor a relative minimum at $$x = 0$$ (Figure 14).

figure.caption: f ′ ( 0 ) = 0 , but f does not have a relative extremum at ( 0 , 0 ) .
figure.alt_text: A curve is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The horizontal axis ranges from around negative 3 to over positive 3 units and the vertical axis ranges from below 6 to beyond 7. The curve y = x^3 enters the third quadrant around (negative 1.9, negative 6.2), bulges away from the negative y axis, slopes upward to the right, and reaches the origin where it levels out and then continues to slope upward to the right, in the first quadrant, bulging away from the y axis and exits the viewing window at around (2, 8).

subsection.paragraph: Second, our result assumes that the function is differentiable and therefore has a derivative at a number that gives rise to a relative extremum. The functions $$f(x) = |x|$$ and $$g(x) = x^{2 \slash 3}$$ demonstrate that a relative extremum of a function may exist at a number at which the derivative does not exist. Both these functions fail to be differentiable at $$x = 0$$ , but each has a relative minimum there. Figure 15 shows the graphs of these functions. Note that the slopes of the tangent lines change from negative to positive as we move across $$x = 0$$ , just as in the case of a function that is differentiable at a value of $$x$$ that gives rise to a relative minimum.

figure.caption: Each of these functions has a relative extremum at ( 0 , 0 ) , but the derivative does not exist there.

In graph a), a symmetric V shaped curve labeled y = |x| enters the second quadrant at around (negative 4, 4), slopes linearly downward to the right, reaches the origin, and from there, it enters the first quadrant and slopes linearly upward to the right and exit the viewing window around (4, 4). The curve labeled y = x^(2/3) enters the second quadrant from the left around (negative 4, 2.5), slopes almost linearly downward to the right, gently bulges upward and reaches the origin. The curve then enters the first quadrant, slopes almost linearly upward to the right, gently bulges up and exits the viewing window at around (4, 2.5).

subsection.paragraph: We refer to a number in the domain of $$f$$ that might give rise to a relative extremum as a critical number.

note.title: Critical Number of f
note.paragraph: A critical number of a function $$f$$ is any number $$x$$ in the domain of $$f$$ such that $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ or $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ does not exist.

subsection.paragraph: Figure 16 depicts the graph of a function that has critical numbers at $$x = a,b,c,d,{and}e$$ . Observe that $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ at $$x = a,b,{and}c$$ . Next, since there is a corner at $$x = d$$ , $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ does not exist there. Finally, $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ does not exist at $$x = e$$ because the tangent line there is vertical. Also, observe that the critical numbers $$x = a,b,{and}d$$ give rise to relative extrema of $$f$$ , whereas the critical numbers $$x = c$$ , and $$x = e$$ do not.

figure.caption: Critical numbers of f
figure.alt_text: A curve is graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. subsection.paragraph: Having defined what a critical number is, we can now state a formal procedure for finding the relative extrema of a continuous function that is differentiable everywhere except at isolated values of $$x$$ . Incorporated into the procedure is the so-called First Derivative Test , which helps us determine whether a number gives rise to a relative maximum or a relative minimum of the function $$f$$ .

subsection.title: Procedure for Finding the Relative Extrema of a Continuous Function f

item.paragraph: Determine the critical numbers of $$f$$ .
Determine the sign of $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ to the left and right of each critical number.
If $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ changes sign from positive to negative as we move across a critical number $$c$$ , then $$f$$ has a relative maximum at $$x = c$$ .
If $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ changes sign from negative to positive as we move across a critical number $$c$$ , then $$f$$ has a relative minimum at $$x = c$$ .
If $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ does not change sign as we move across a critical number $$c$$ , then $$f$$ does not have a relative extremum at $$x = c$$ .

problem.paragraph: Find the relative maxima and relative minima of the function $$f(x) = x^{2}$$ .

solution.paragraph: The derivative of $$f(x) = x^{2}$$ is given by $$f^{\prime}(x) = 2x$$ . Setting $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ yields $$x = 0$$ as the only critical number of $$f$$ . Since
and
we see that $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ changes sign from negative to positive as we move across the critical number $$0$$ . Thus, we conclude that $$f(0) = 0$$ is a relative minimum of $$f$$ (Figure 17).

problem.paragraph: Find the relative maxima and relative minima of the function $$f(x) = x^{2 \slash 3}$$ (see Example 3).

solution.paragraph: The derivative of $$f$$ is $$f^{\prime}(x) = \frac{2}{3}‍x^{- 1 \slash 3}$$ . As was noted in Example 3, $$f^{\prime}$$ is not defined at $$x = 0$$ , is continuous everywhere else, and is not equal to zero in its domain. Thus, $$x = 0$$ is the only critical number of the function $$f$$ .

The sign diagram obtained in Example 3 is reproduced in Figure 18. We can see that the sign of $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ changes from negative to positive as we move across $$x = 0$$ from left to right. Thus, an application of the First Derivative Test tells us that $$f(0) = 0$$ is a relative minimum of $$f$$ (Figure 19).

The graph of the function $$f$$ , shown in the accompanying figure, is referred to as a “bathtub curve” in the airline industry. It gives the fleet damage rate (damage due to corrosion, accident, and metal fatigue) of a typical fleet of commercial aircraft as a function of the number of years of service.

subsection.title: Using Technology Using the First Derivative to Analyze a Function
subsection.paragraph: A graphing utility is an effective tool for analyzing the properties of functions. This is especially true when we also bring into play the power of calculus, as the following examples show.

item.paragraph: Use a graphing utility to plot the graph of $$f$$ .
Find the intervals where $$f$$ is increasing and the intervals where $$f$$ is decreasing.
Find the relative extrema of $$f$$ .
The graph of $$f$$ in the viewing window $$\left\lbrack {- 2,4} \right\rbrack \times \left\lbrack {- 10,10} \right\rbrack$$ is shown in Figure T1.

figure.caption: The graph of f in the viewing window [ - 2 , 4 ] × [ - 10 , 10 ]
figure.alt_text: A curve is graphed on the coordinate plane in the viewing window. The horizontal axis ranges from negative 2 to positive 2 and the vertical axis ranges from negative 10 to positive 10. The curve enters the second quadrant at around (negative 1, 10), slopes downward to the right, follows almost a straight path till (0.7, 1), then bulges down, cuts the vertical axis around (0, 1) and enters the first quadrant. It then bulges up and reaches the point around (0.6, 2), then it slopes downward and cuts the horizontal axis around (1.2, 0), enters the fourth quadrant. After it reaches the point around (1.5, negative 4), it slopes downward and bulges down, reaches the low point around (2.2, negative 8.2), where it turns up to the right, cuts the x axis around (2.7, 0), and enters the first quadrant and exits the viewing window around (3, 10).

item.paragraph: We compute

and observe that $$f^{\prime}$$ is continuous everywhere, so the critical numbers of $$f$$ occur at values of $$x$$ where $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ . To solve this last equation, observe that $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ is a polynomial function of degree $$3$$ . The easiest way to solve the polynomial equation

is to use the function on a graphing utility for solving polynomial equations. (Not all graphing utilities have this function.) You can also use trace and zoom, but this will not give the same accuracy without a much greater effort.
We find

Referring to Figure T1, we conclude that $$f$$ is decreasing on $$\left( {- \infty, - 0.2959} \right)$$ and $$\left( {0.6327,2.2256} \right)$$ (correct to four decimal places) and $$f$$ is increasing on $$\left( {- 0.2959,0.6327} \right)$$ and $$\left( {2.2256,\infty} \right)$$ .

Using the evaluation function of a graphing utility, we find the value of $$f$$ at each of the critical numbers found in part (b). Upon referring to Figure T1 once again, we see that $$f\left( x_{3} \right) \approx 0.2836$$ and $$f\left( x_{1} \right) \approx - 8.2366$$ are relative minimum values of $$f$$ and $$f\left( x_{2} \right) \approx 2.9194$$ is a relative maximum value of $$f$$ .

note.title: Note
note.paragraph: The equation $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ in Example 1 is a polynomial equation, so it is easily solved by using the function for solving polynomial equations. We could also solve the equation using the function for finding the roots of equations, but that would require much more work. For equations that are not polynomial equations, however, our only choice is to use the function for finding the roots of equations.

subsection.paragraph: If the derivative of a function is difficult to compute or simplify and we do not require great precision in the solution, we can find the relative extrema of the function using a combination of zoom and trace. This technique, which does not require the use of the derivative of $$f$$ , is illustrated in the following example.

item.paragraph: Use a graphing utility to plot the graph of $$f$$ .*
Find the relative extrema of $$f$$ .
The graph of $$f$$ in the viewing window $$\left\lbrack {- 4,2} \right\rbrack \times \left\lbrack {- 2,1} \right\rbrack$$ is shown in Figure T2.

From the graph of $$f$$ in Figure T2, we see that $$f$$ has relative maxima when $$x \approx - 2$$ and $$x \approx 0.25$$ and a relative minimum when $$x \approx - 0.75$$ . To obtain a better approximation of the first relative maximum, we zoom in with the cursor at approximately the point on the graph corresponding to $$x \approx - 2$$ . Then, using trace, we see that a relative maximum occurs when $$x \approx - 1.76$$ with value $$y \approx - 1.01$$ . Similarly, we find the other relative maximum where $$x \approx 0.20$$ with value $$y \approx 0.44$$ . Repeating the procedure, we find the relative minimum at $$x \approx - 0.86$$ and $$y \approx - 1.07$$ .

figure.caption: The graph of f in the viewing window [ - 4 , 2 ] × [ - 2 , 1 ]
figure.alt_text: A curve is graphed on the coordinate plane in the viewing window. The horizontal axis ranges from negative 4 to positive 2 and the vertical axis ranges from negative 2 to positive 1. The curve enters the viewing window around (negative 4, negative 1.8), slopes upward to the right, bulges up till it reaches the low point around (negative 1.76, negative 1.01), then it slightly bulges down till it reaches around (negative 0.86, negative 1.07), then it slopes steeply upward to the right and passes through the origin. Then it, runs very close to the vertical axis, enters the first quadrant slopes upward, bulges up and reaches the high point around (0.20, 0.44), inflects, it slopes downward bulging down and meets the horizontal axis at around (1.5, 0).

subsection.paragraph: You can also use the “minimum” and “maximum” functions of a graphing utility to find the relative extrema of the function. See the website for the procedure.

Finally, we comment that if you have access to a computer and software such as Derive, Maple, or Mathematica, then symbolic differentiation will yield the derivative $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ of a differentiable function. This software will also solve the equation $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ with ease. Thus, the use of a computer will simplify even more greatly the analysis of functions.

subsection.title: Determining the Intervals of Concavity
subsection.paragraph: Consider the graphs shown in Figure 26, which give the estimated population of the world and of the United States through the year 2000. Both graphs are rising, indicating that both the U.S. population and the world population continued to increase through the year 2000. But observe that the graph in Figure 26a opens upward, whereas the graph in Figure 26b opens downward. What is the significance of this? To answer this question, let’s look at the slopes of the tangent lines to various points on each graph (Figure 27).

subsection.paragraph: In Figure 27a, we see that the slopes of the tangent lines to the graph are increasing as we move from left to right. Since the slope of the tangent line to the graph at a point on the graph measures the rate of change of the function at that point, we conclude that the world population not only was increasing through the year 2000 but also was increasing at an increasing pace. A similar analysis of Figure 27b reveals that the U.S. population was increasing, but at a decreasing pace.
The shape of a curve can be described by using the notion of concavity.

note.title: Concavity of a Function f
note.paragraph: Let the function $$f$$ be differentiable on an interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ . Then,

item.paragraph: The graph of $$f$$ is concave upward on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ if $$f^{\prime}$$ is increasing on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ .
The graph of $$f$$ is concave downward on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ if $$f^{\prime}$$ is decreasing on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ .

subsection.paragraph: Geometrically, a curve is concave upward if it lies above its tangent lines (Figure 28a). Similarly, a curve is concave downward if it lies below its tangent lines (Figure 28b).

figure.alt_text: Two graphs a and b, each plot a curve on the x y coordinate plane. The horizontal axis has tick marks labeled a and b. In graph a, two vertical lines are drawn perpendicular to the x axis meet at the labeled marks a and b. The U shaped curve starts very close and to the right of the line, slopes downward to the right, concave up, reaches the low point, from where it turns upward to the right, still concave up and reaches to the left of the vertical line. Four slanting lines are drawn at the turning point to the left side of the curve; two on the left side of the curve and two on the right such that the curve lies above the tangent lines. The tangent at the lower part of the curve rises gradually upward to the right and the tangent at the upper part of the curve rises even more steeply upward to the right. In graph b, the inverted U shaped curve starts above the horizontal axis, slopes upward to the right, follows almost a linear path, then it slightly concave down, after it inflects, slopes downward, follows almost a linear path. Two vertical lines drawn from the entry point and end point of the curve to meet the x axis labeled at marks a and b. Four slanting lines are drawn at the turning point to the left side of the curve; two on the left side of the curve and two on the right such that the curve lies below the tangent lines. The tangent at the lower part of the curve rises gradually upward to the right and the tangent at the upper part of the curve rises even more steeply upward to the right.

subsection.paragraph: We also say that the graph of $$f$$ is concave upward at a number $$c$$ if there exists an interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ containing $$c$$ on which the graph of $$f$$ is concave upward. Similarly, we say that the graph of $$f$$ is concave downward at a number $$c$$ if there exists an interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ containing $$c$$ on which the graph of $$f$$ is concave downward.

If a function $$f$$ has a second derivative $$f^{''}$$ , we can use $$f^{''}$$ to determine the intervals of concavity of the graph of the function. Recall that $$f^{''}(x)$$ measures the rate of change of the slope $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ of the tangent line to the graph of $$f$$ at the point $$\left( {x,f(x)} \right)$$ . Thus, if $$f^{''}(x) > 0$$ on an interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ , then the slopes of the tangent lines to the graph of $$f$$ are increasing on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ , so the graph of $$f$$ is concave upward on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ . Similarly, if $$f^{''}(x) < 0$$ on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ , then the graph of $$f$$ is concave downward on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ . These observations suggest the following theorem.

item.paragraph: If $$f^{''}(x) > 0$$ for every value of $$x$$ in $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ , then the graph of $$f$$ is concave upward on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ .
If $$f^{''}(x) < 0$$ for every value of $$x$$ in $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ , then the graph of $$f$$ is concave downward on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ .

subsection.paragraph: The following procedure, based on the conclusions of Theorem 2, may be used to determine the intervals of concavity of the graph of a function.

note.title: Determining the Intervals of Concavity of the Graph of f

item.paragraph: Determine the values of $$x$$ for which $$f^{''}$$ is zero or where $$f^{''}$$ is not defined, and identify the open intervals determined by these numbers.
Determine the sign of $$f^{''}$$ in each interval found in Step 1. To do this, compute $$f^{''}(c)$$ , where $$c$$ is any conveniently chosen test number in the interval.
If $$f^{''}(c) > 0$$ , then the graph of $$f$$ is concave upward on that interval.
If $$f^{''}(c) < 0$$ , then the graph of $$f$$ is concave downward on that interval.

subsection.title: Inflection Points
subsection.paragraph: Figure 33 shows the total sales $$S$$ of a manufacturer of automobile air conditioners versus the amount of money $$x$$ that the company spends on advertising its product.

figure.caption: The graph of S has a point of inflection at ( 50 , 2700 ) .
figure.alt_text: A curve y = S(x) is graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The x axis ranges from 0 to over 100 (thousands of dollars) with the tick marks on the x axis increasing in increments of 20. The y axis ranges from 0 to over 5000 (thousands of dollars) with the tick marks on the y axis increasing in increments of 1000. The curve begins with a low at the y axis, very close to the origin, slightly above it, goes up to the right, concave up and reaches its point of inflection at a point marked (50, 2700) and then continues to rise upward to the right, now concave down, till it reaches its high point at around (100, 5000).

subsection.paragraph: Notice that the graph of the continuous function $$y = S(x)$$ changes concavity—from upward to downward—at the point $$\left( {50,2700} \right)$$ . This point is called an inflection point of $$S$$ . To understand the significance of this inflection point, observe that the total sales increase rather slowly at first, but as more money is spent on advertising, the total sales increase rapidly. This rapid increase reflects the effectiveness of the company’s ads. However, a point is soon reached after which any additional advertising expenditure results in increased sales but at a slower rate of increase. This point, commonly known as the point of diminishing returns, is the point of inflection of the function $$S$$ . We will return to this example later.
Let’s now state formally the definition of an inflection point.

note.title: Inflection Point
note.paragraph: A point on the graph of a continuous function $$f$$ where the tangent line exists and where the concavity changes is called a point of inflection or an inflection point .

subsection.paragraph: Observe that the graph of a function crosses its tangent line at a point of inflection (Figure 34).

subsection.paragraph: The following procedure may be used to find inflection points:

item.paragraph: Compute $$f^{''}(x)$$ .
Determine the numbers in the domain of $$f$$ for which $$f^{''}(x) = 0$$ or $$f^{''}(x)$$ does not exist.

Determine the sign of $$f^{''}(x)$$ to the left and right of each number $$c$$ found in Step 2. If there is a change in the sign of $$f^{''}(x)$$ as we move across $$x = c$$ , then $$\left( {c,f(c)} \right)$$ is an inflection point of $$f$$ .

subsection.paragraph: The numbers that were found in Step 2 are only candidates for the inflection points of $$f$$ . For example, you can easily verify that $$f^{''}(0) = 0$$ if $$f(x) = x^{4}$$ , but a sketch of the graph of $$f$$ will show that $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ is not an inflection point.

subsection.paragraph: The next example uses an interpretation of the first and second derivatives to help us sketch the graph of a function.

problem.paragraph: Sketch the graph of a function having the following properties:

solution.paragraph: First, we plot the points $$\left( {- 1,4} \right)$$ , $$\left( {0,2} \right)$$ , and $$\left( {1,0} \right)$$ that lie on the graph of $$f$$ . Since $$f^{\prime}\left( {- 1} \right) = 0$$ and $$f^{\prime}(1) = 0$$ , the tangent lines at the points $$\left( {- 1,4} \right)$$ and $$\left( {1,0} \right)$$ are horizontal. Since $$f^{\prime}(x) > 0$$ on $$\left( {- \infty, - 1} \right)$$ and $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ on $$\left( {- 1,1} \right)$$ , we see that $$f$$ has a relative maximum at the point $$\left( {- 1,4} \right)$$ . Also, $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ on $$\left( {- 1,1} \right)$$ and $$f^{\prime}(x) > 0$$ on $$\left( {1,\infty} \right)$$ implies that $$f$$ has a relative minimum at the point $$\left( {1,0} \right)$$ (Figure 41a).

Since $$f^{''}(x) < 0$$ on $$\left( {- \infty,0} \right)$$ and $$f^{''}(x) > 0$$ on $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ , we see that the point $$\left( {0,2} \right)$$ is an inflection point. Finally, we complete the graph, making use of the fact that $$f$$ is increasing on $$\left( {- \infty, - 1} \right)$$ and $$\left( {1,\infty} \right)$$ , where it is given that $$f^{\prime}(x) > 0$$ , and $$f$$ is decreasing on $$\left( {- 1,1} \right)$$ , where $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ . Also, make sure that the graph of $$f$$ is concave downward on $$\left( {- \infty,0} \right)$$ and concave upward on $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ (Figure 41b).

subsection.title: The Second Derivative Test
subsection.paragraph: We now show how the second derivative $$f^{''}$$ of a function $$f$$ can be used to help us determine whether a critical number of $$f$$ gives rise to a relative extremum of $$f$$ . Figure 43a shows the graph of a function that has a relative maximum at $$x = c$$ . Observe that the graph of $$f$$ is concave downward at that number. Similarly, Figure 43b shows that at a relative minimum of $$f$$ , the graph is concave upward. But from our previous work, we know that the graph of $$f$$ is concave downward at $$x = c$$ if $$f^{''}(c) < 0$$ and the graph of $$f$$ is concave upward at $$x = c$$ if $$f^{''}(c) > 0$$ . These observations suggest the following alternative procedure for determining whether a critical number of $$f$$ gives rise to a relative extremum of $$f$$ . This result is called the Second Derivative Test and is applicable when $$f^{''}$$ exists.

subsection.title: Comparing the First and Second Derivative Tests
subsection.paragraph: Notice that both the First Derivative Test and the Second Derivative Test are used to classify the critical numbers of $$f$$ . What are the pros and cons of the two tests? Since the Second Derivative Test is applicable only when $$f^{''}$$ exists, it is less versatile than the First Derivative Test. For example, it cannot be used to locate the relative minimum $$f(0) = 0$$ of the function $$f(x) = x^{2 \slash 3}$$ .

Furthermore, the Second Derivative Test is inconclusive when $$f^{''}$$ is equal to zero at a critical number of $$f$$ , whereas the First Derivative Test always yields a conclusion; that is, it tells us if $$f$$ has a relative maximum, relative minimum, or neither. The Second Derivative Test is also inconvenient to use when $$f^{''}$$ is difficult to compute. On the plus side, if $$f^{''}$$ is computed easily, then we use the Second Derivative Test, since it involves just the evaluation of $$f^{''}$$ at the critical number(s) of $$f$$ . Also, the conclusions of the Second Derivative Test are important in theoretical work.

We close this section by summarizing the different roles played by the first derivative $$f^{\prime}$$ and the second derivative $$f^{''}$$ of a function $$f$$ in determining the properties of the graph of $$f$$ . The first derivative $$f^{\prime}$$ tells us where $$f$$ is increasing and where $$f$$ is decreasing, whereas the second derivative $$f^{''}$$ tells us where the graph of $$f$$ is concave upward and where it is concave downward. These different properties of $$f$$ are reflected by the signs of $$f^{\prime}$$ and $$f^{''}$$ in the interval of interest. subsection.title: A Real-Life Example
subsection.paragraph: As we have seen on numerous occasions, the graph of a function is a useful aid for visualizing the function’s properties. From a practical point of view, the graph of a function also gives, at one glance, a complete summary of all the information captured by the function.

Consider, for example, the graph of the function giving the Dow-Jones Industrial Average (DJIA) on Black Monday, October 19, 1987 (Figure 44). Here, $$t = 0$$ corresponds to 9:30 a.m., when the market was open for business, and $$t = 6.5$$ corresponds to 4 p.m., the closing time. The following information may be gleaned from studying the graph.

figure.caption: The Dow-Jones Industrial Average on Black Monday
figure.alt_text: A curve is graphed in a coordinate plane. The horizontal axis t is marked from 0 to 7 hours in increments 1 hour. The y axis labeled DJIA is marked from 1700 to 2200 in increments of 100. There is an axis breaker in between 0 and 1700. The curve begins at a marked point (0, 2164), descends downward to the right, concave up, reaches a low point at the marked point (1, 2047), rises upward to the right till approximately (1.5, 2100) where it inflects. From here, the curve rises upward to the right, concave down, reaches a high point at the marked point(2, 2150) and then descends till about (3, 2090) where it inflects again and then descends downward concave up. The curve then reaches a low point at a marked point (4, 2006), levels out and runs parallel to the horizontal axis till (5, 2006), and then descends downward, concave down till the marked point (6.5, 1739).

subsection.paragraph: The graph is falling rapidly from $$t = 0$$ to $$t = 1$$ , reflecting the sharp drop in the index in the first hour of trading. The point $$\left( {1,2047} \right)$$ is a relative minimum point of the function, and this turning point coincides with the start of an aborted recovery. The short-lived rally, represented by the portion of the graph that is rising on the interval $$\left( {1,2} \right)$$ , quickly fizzled out at $$t = 2$$ (11:30 a.m.). The relative maximum point $$\left( {2,2150} \right)$$ marks the highest point of the recovery. The function is decreasing in the rest of the interval. The point $$\left( {4,2006} \right)$$ is an inflection point of the function; it shows that there was a temporary respite at $$t = 4$$ (1:30 p.m.). However, selling pressure continued unabated, and the DJIA continued to fall until the closing bell. Finally, the graph also shows that the index opened at the high of the day [$$f(0) = 2164$$ is the absolute maximum of the function] and closed at the low of the day [$$f\left( \frac{13}{2} \right) = 1739$$ is the absolute minimum of the function], a drop of $$508$$ points from the previous close!*
Before we turn our attention to the actual task of sketching the graph of a function, let’s look at some properties of graphs that will be helpful in this connection.

subsection.paragraph: Before going on, you might want to review the material on one-sided limits and the limit at infinity of a function (Section 2.4 and 2.5).

subsection.paragraph: You can verify this by taking a sequence of values of $$x$$ approaching $$x = 1$$ from the right and looking at the corresponding values of $$f(x)$$ .

Here is another way of looking at the situation: Observe that if $$x$$ is a number that is a little larger than $$1$$ , then both $$\left( {x + 1} \right)$$ and $$\left( {x - 1} \right)$$ are positive, so $$\left( {x + 1} \right) \slash \left( {x - 1} \right)$$ is also positive. As $$x$$ approaches $$x = 1$$ , the numerator $$\left( {x + 1} \right)$$ approaches the number $$2$$ , but the denominator $$\left( {x - 1} \right)$$ approaches zero, so the quotient $$\left( {x + 1} \right) \slash \left( {x - 1} \right)$$ approaches infinity, as observed earlier. The line $$x = 1$$ is called a vertical asymptote of the graph of $$f$$ .

note.paragraph: Although a vertical asymptote of a graph is not part of the graph, it serves as a useful aid for sketching the graph.

subsection.paragraph: For rational functions
there is a simple criterion for determining whether the graph of $$f$$ has any vertical asymptotes.

note.title: Finding Vertical Asymptotes of Rational Functions
note.paragraph: Suppose $$f$$ is a rational function
where $$P$$ and $$Q$$ are polynomial functions. Then, the line $$x = a$$ is a vertical asymptote of the graph of $$f$$ if $$Q(a) = 0$$ but $$P(a) \neq 0$$ .

considered earlier, $$P(x) = x + 1$$ and $$Q(x) = x - 1$$ . Observe that $$Q(1) = 0$$ but $$P(1) = 2 \neq 0$$ , so $$x = 1$$ is a vertical asymptote of the graph of $$f$$ .

subsection.paragraph: We next state an important property of polynomial functions.
To see this, note that a polynomial function $$P(x)$$ can be written as a rational function with denominator equal to $$1$$ . Thus,
Since the denominator is never equal to zero, $$P$$ has no vertical asymptotes. Next, if $$P$$ is a polynomial of degree greater than or equal to $$1$$ , then
and
are either infinity or minus infinity; that is, they do not exist. Therefore, $$P$$ has no horizontal asymptotes.

In Section 4.1 and 4.2, we saw how the first and second derivatives of a function are used to reveal various properties of the graph of a function $$f$$ . We now show how this information can be used to help us sketch the graph of $$f$$ . We begin by giving a general procedure for curve sketching.

item.paragraph: Determine the domain of $$f$$ .
Find the $$x$$ - and $$y$$ -intercepts of $$f$$ .*
Determine the behavior of $$f$$ for large absolute values of $$x$$ .
Find all horizontal and vertical asymptotes of the graph of $$f$$ .
Determine the intervals where $$f$$ is increasing and where $$f$$ is decreasing.
Find the relative extrema of $$f$$ .
Determine the concavity of the graph of $$f$$ .
Find the inflection points of $$f$$ .
Plot a few additional points to help further identify the shape of the graph of $$f$$ and sketch the graph.

note.paragraph: The average price of gasoline at the pump over a $$3$$-month period, during which there was a temporary shortage of oil, is described by the function $$f$$ defined on the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,3} \right\rbrack$$ . During the first month, the price was increasing at an increasing rate. Starting with the second month, the good news was that the rate of increase was slowing down, although the price of gas was still increasing. This pattern continued until the end of the second month. The price of gas peaked at $$t = 2$$ and began to fall at an increasing rate until $$t = 3$$ .

subsection.title: Using Technology Analyzing the Properties of a Function
subsection.paragraph: One of the main purposes of studying Section 4.3 is to see how the many concepts of calculus come together to paint a picture of a function. The techniques of graphing also play a very practical role. For example, using the techniques of graphing developed in Section 4.3, you can tell whether the graph of a function generated by a graphing utility is reasonably complete. Furthermore, these techniques can often reveal details that are missing from a graph.

problem.paragraph: Consider the function $$f(x) = 2x^{3} - 3.5x^{2} + x - 10$$ . A plot of the graph of $$f$$ in the standard viewing window is shown in Figure T1. Since the domain of $$f$$ is the interval $$\left( {- \infty,\infty} \right)$$ , we see that Figure T1 does not reveal the part of the graph to the left of the $$y$$ -axis. This suggests that we enlarge the viewing window accordingly. Figure T2 shows the graph of $$f$$ in the viewing window $$\left\lbrack {- 10,10} \right\rbrack \times \left\lbrack {- 20,10} \right\rbrack$$ .

subsection.title: Finding x -Intercepts
subsection.paragraph: As was noted in Section 4.3, it is not always easy to find the $$x$$ -intercepts of the graph of a function. But this information is very important in applications. By using the function for solving polynomial equations or the function for finding the roots of an equation, we can solve the equation $$f(x) = 0$$ quite easily and hence yield the $$x$$ -intercepts of the graph of a function.

note.title: Note
note.paragraph: The function for solving polynomial equations on a graphing utility will solve a polynomial equation $$f(x) = 0$$ , where $$f$$ is a polynomial function. The function for finding the roots of an equation, however, will solve equations $$f(x) = 0$$ even if $$f$$ is not a polynomial.

subsection.title: Absolute Extrema
subsection.paragraph: The graph of the function $$f$$ in Figure 56 shows the average age of cars in use in the United States from the beginning of 1946 $$\left( {t = 0} \right)$$ to the beginning of 2009 $$\left( {t = 63} \right)$$ . Observe that the highest average age of cars in use during this period is $$9.3$$ years, whereas the lowest average age of cars in use during the same period is $$5.5$$ years. The number $$9.3$$ , the largest value of $$f(t)$$ for all values of $$t$$ in the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,63} \right\rbrack$$ (the domain of $$f$$ ), is called the absolute maximum value of $$f$$ on that interval. The number $$5.5$$ , the smallest value of $$f(t)$$ for all values of $$t$$ in $$\left\lbrack {0,63} \right\rbrack$$ , is called the absolute minimum value of $$f$$ on that interval. Notice, too, that the absolute maximum value of $$f$$ is attained at the endpoint $$t = 63$$ of the interval, whereas the absolute minimum value of $$f$$ is attained at the points $$t = 12$$ (corresponding to 1958) and $$t = 23$$ (corresponding to 1969) that lie within the interval $$\left( {0,63} \right)$$ .

subsection.paragraph: (Incidentally, it is interesting to note that 1946 marked the first year of peace following World War II and the two years 1958 and 1969 marked the end of two periods of prosperity in recent U.S. history.)
A precise definition of the absolute extrema (absolute maximum or absolute minimum) of a function follows.

note.title: The Absolute Extrema of a Function f
note.paragraph: If $$f(x) \leq f(c)$$ for all $$x$$ in the domain of $$f$$ , then $$f(c)$$ is called the absolute maximum value of $$f$$ .
If $$f(x) \geq f(c)$$ for all $$x$$ in the domain of $$f$$ , then $$f(c)$$ is called the absolute minimum value of $$f$$ .

subsection.title: Absolute Extrema on a Closed Interval
subsection.paragraph: As the preceding examples show, a continuous function defined on an arbitrary interval does not always have an absolute maximum or an absolute minimum. But an important case arises often in practical applications in which both the absolute maximum and the absolute minimum of a function are guaranteed to exist. This occurs when a continuous function is defined on a closed interval.

Before stating this important result formally, let’s look at a real-life example. The graph of the function $$f$$ in Figure 58 shows the average price, $$f(t)$$ , in dollars, of domestic airfares by days before flight. The domain of $$f$$ is the closed interval $$\lbrack - 210, - 1\rbrack$$ , where $$- 210$$ is interpreted as $$210$$ days before flight and $$- 1$$ is interpreted as the day before flight.

figure.caption: Average price before flight
figure.alt_text: A curve is graphed on a coordinate plane. The horizontal axis t is marked from negative 200 to 0 in increments of 50 days. The vertical axis y is marked from 300 to 700 in increments of 100 dollars. There is an axis breaker just below the mark 300 on the vertical axis. The curve begins with a filled dot at (negative 200, 550), descends gradually to the right, concave up, reaching a low point at (negative 50, 400), and then rises upward rapidly to the right, till around (negative 5, 600) where it ends with a filled dot.

subsection.paragraph: Observe that $$f$$ attains the minimum value of $$395$$ when $$t = - 49$$ and the maximum value of $$614$$ when $$t = - 1$$ . This result tells us that the best time to book a domestic flight is seven weeks in advance and the worst day to book a domestic flight is the day before the flight. Probably most surprising of all, booking too early can be almost as expensive as booking too late. Note that the function $$f$$ is continuous on a closed interval. For such functions, we have the following theorem.

note.paragraph: If a function $$f$$ is continuous on a closed interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ , then $$f$$ has both an absolute maximum value and an absolute minimum value on $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ .

subsection.paragraph: Observe that if an absolute extremum of a continuous function $$f$$ occurs at a point in an open interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ , then it must be a relative extremum of $$f$$ , and hence its $$x$$ -coordinate must be a critical number of $$f$$ . Otherwise, the absolute extremum of $$f$$ must occur at one or both of the endpoints of the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ . A typical situation is illustrated in Figure 59.

From the relative minimum, the curve rises a bit more steeply to the right, concave up, to reach a high point marked with a filled dot and labeled relative maximum. The graph then descends gradually to the right, concave up, and reaches a low point, below all other marked points, marked with a filled dot and labeled Absolute minimum. subsection.paragraph: Here, $$x_{1}$$ , $$x_{2}$$ , and $$x_{3}$$ are critical numbers of $$f$$ . The absolute minimum of $$f$$ occurs at $$x_{3}$$ , which lies in the open interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ and is a critical number of $$f$$ . The absolute maximum of $$f$$ occurs at $$b$$ , an endpoint. This observation suggests the following procedure for finding the absolute extrema of a continuous function on a closed interval.

note.title: Finding the Absolute Extrema of f on a Closed Interval

The absolute maximum value and absolute minimum value of $$f$$ will correspond to the largest and smallest numbers, respectively, found in Step 2.

subsection.paragraph: Many real-world applications call for finding the absolute maximum value or the absolute minimum value of a given function. For example, management is interested in finding what level of production will yield the maximum profit for a company; a farmer is interested in finding the right amount of fertilizer to maximize crop yield; a doctor is interested in finding the maximum concentration of a drug in a patient’s body and the time at which it occurs; and an engineer is interested in finding the dimensions of a container with a specified shape and volume that can be constructed at a minimum cost.

statement.paragraph: If $$f$$ is not continuous on the closed interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ , then $$f$$ cannot have an absolute maximum value.

item.paragraph: True
False

statement.paragraph: If $$f$$ is defined on a closed interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ , then $$f$$ has an absolute maximum value.

item.paragraph: True
False

statement.paragraph: If $$f^{''}(x) < 0$$ on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ and $$f^{\prime}(c) = 0$$ , where $$a < c < b$$ , then $$f(c)$$ is the absolute maximum value of $$f$$ on $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ .

item.paragraph: True
False

statement.paragraph: If $$f$$ is continuous on $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ , $$f$$ is differentiable on $$(a,b)$$ , and $$f^{\prime}(x) \neq 0$$ for all $$x$$ in $$(a,b)$$ , then the absolute maximum value of $$f$$ on $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ is $$f(a)$$ or $$f(b)$$ .

item.paragraph: True
False

statement.paragraph: If $$f$$ is continuous on $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ , $$f$$ is differentiable on $$(a,b)$$ , and $$f^{\prime}(x) > 0$$ for all $$x$$ in $$(a,b)$$ , then the absolute minimum value of $$f$$ on $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ is $$f(a)$$ .

item.paragraph: True
False

item.paragraph: True
False

item.paragraph: True
False

subsection.title: Using Technology Finding the Absolute Extrema of a Function
subsection.paragraph: Some graphing utilities have a function for finding the absolute maximum and the absolute minimum values of a continuous function on a closed interval. If your graphing utility has this capability, use it to work through the example and exercises of this section.

problem.paragraph: Let $$f(x) = \frac{2x + 4}{\left( x^{2} + 1 \right)^{3 \slash 2}}$$ .

Find the absolute maximum and absolute minimum values of $$f$$ on the interval $$\left\lbrack {- 3,3} \right\rbrack$$ . Express your answers accurate to four decimal places.
The graph of $$f$$ is shown in Figure T1.

figure.caption: The graph of f in the viewing window [ - 3 , 3 ] × [ - 1 , 5 ]

The curve runs along the horizontal axis in the viewing window from negative 3 till negative 2 mark, it then slopes upward to the right, concave up till it inflects around (negative 0.5, 2), then it slopes upward, concave down, cuts the vertical axis at (0, 4), slopes upward, reaches the highest point at around (0.2, 4.2). Then it slopes downward to the right, still concave down, after it inflects around (0.8, 2.5), it slopes downward to the right, concave up and ends around (3, 0.4) in the viewing window.

item.paragraph: Using the function on a graphing utility for finding the absolute minimum value of a continuous function on a closed interval, we find the absolute minimum value of $$f$$ to be $$- 0.0632$$ . Similarly, using the function for finding the absolute maximum value, we find the absolute maximum value to be $$4.1593$$ .

note.title: Note
note.paragraph: Some graphing utilities will enable you to find the absolute minimum and absolute maximum values of a continuous function on a closed interval without having to graph the function. For example, using fMax on the TI-83/84 will yield the $$x$$ -coordinate of the absolute maximum of $$f$$ . The absolute maximum value can then be found by evaluating $$f$$ at that value of $$x$$ . Figure T2 shows the work involved in finding the absolute maximum of the function of Example 1.

content.paragraph: In Section 4.4, we outlined a method for finding the solution to certain optimization problems in which the objective function is given. In this section, we consider problems in which we are required to first find the appropriate function to be optimized. The following guidelines will be useful for solving these problems.

item.paragraph: Assign a letter to each variable mentioned in the problem. If appropriate, draw and label a figure.
Find an expression for the quantity to be optimized.

Use the conditions given in the problem to write the quantity to be optimized as a function $$f$$ of one variable. Note any restrictions to be placed on the domain of $$f$$ from physical considerations of the problem.
Optimize the function $$f$$ over its domain using the methods of Section 4.4.

note.title: Note
note.paragraph: In carrying out Step 4, remember that if the function $$f$$ to be optimized is continuous on a closed interval, then the absolute maximum and absolute minimum of $$f$$ are, respectively, the largest and smallest values of $$f(x)$$ on the set composed of the critical numbers of $$f$$ and the endpoints of the interval. If the domain of $$f$$ is not a closed interval, then we resort to the graphical or some other method.

note.title: Applied Example 3. Optimal Subway Fare
note.paragraph: A city’s Metropolitan Transit Authority (MTA) operates a subway line for commuters from a certain suburb to the downtown metropolitan area. Currently, an average of $$6000$$ passengers a day take the trains, paying a fare of $$\$ 3.00$$ per ride. The board of the MTA, contemplating raising the fare to $$\$ 3.50$$ per ride in order to generate a larger revenue, engages the services of a consulting firm. The firm’s study reveals that for each $$\$ 0.50$$ increase in fare, the ridership will be reduced by an average of $$1000$$ passengers a day. Therefore, the consulting firm recommends that MTA stick to the current fare of $$\$ 3.00$$ per ride, which already yields a maximum revenue. Show that the consultants are correct.

subsection.title: An Inventory Problem
subsection.paragraph: One problem faced by many companies is that of controlling the inventory of goods carried. Ideally, the manager must ensure that the company has sufficient stock to meet customer demand at all times. At the same time, she must make sure that this is accomplished without overstocking (incurring unnecessary storage costs) and also without having to place orders too frequently (incurring reordering costs).

note.title: Applied Example 5. Inventory Control and Planning
note.paragraph: Dixie Import-Export is the sole agent for the Excalibur $$250$$-cc motorcycle. Management estimates that the demand for these motorcycles is $$10,000$$ per year and that they will sell at a uniform rate throughout the year. The cost incurred in ordering each shipment of motorcycles is $$\$ 10,000$$ , and the cost per year of storing each motorcycle is $$\$ 200$$ .

Dixie’s management faces the following problem: Ordering too many motorcycles at one time ties up valuable storage space and increases the storage cost. On the other hand, placing orders too frequently increases the ordering costs. How large should each order be, and how often should orders be placed, to minimize ordering and storage costs?

subsection.title: Solution
subsection.paragraph: Let $$x$$ denote the number of motorcycles in each order (the lot size). Then, assuming that each shipment arrives just as the previous shipment has been sold, the average number of motorcycles in storage during the year is $$x \slash 2$$ . You can see that this is the case by examining Figure 73. Thus, Dixie’s storage cost for the year is given by $$200\left( {x \slash 2} \right)$$ , or $$100x$$ dollars.
Next, since the company requires $$10,000$$ motorcycles for the year and since each order is for $$x$$ motorcycles, the number of orders required is
This gives an ordering cost of
dollars for the year. Thus, the total yearly cost incurred by Dixie, which includes the ordering and storage costs attributed to the sale of these motorcycles, is given by
The problem is reduced to finding the absolute minimum of the function $$C$$ on the interval $$\left( \left. {0,10,000} \right\rbrack \right.$$ . To accomplish this, we compute

Setting $$C^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ and solving the resulting equation, we obtain $$x = \pm 1000$$ . Since the number $$- 1000$$ is outside the domain of the function $$C$$ , it is rejected, leaving $$1000$$ as the only critical number of $$C$$ . Next, we find

Since $$C^{''}(1000) > 0$$ , the Second Derivative Test implies that the critical number $$1000$$ is a relative minimum of the function $$C$$ (Figure 74). Also, since $$C^{''}(x) > 0$$ for all $$x$$ in $$\left( {0,10,000} \right)$$ , the graph of $$C$$ is concave upward everywhere, so $$x = 1000$$ also gives the absolute minimum of $$C$$ . Thus, to minimize the ordering and storage costs, Dixie should place $$10,000 \slash 1000$$ , or $$10$$ , orders a year, each for a shipment of $$1000$$ motorcycles.

Since the area is to be $$300{ft}^{2}$$ , we have

Setting $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ yields $$x = - \sqrt{300}$$ or $$x = \sqrt{300}$$ . We consider only the critical number $$\sqrt{300}$$ , since $$- \sqrt{300}$$ lies outside the interval $$(0,\infty)$$ . We then compute

In fact, since $$f^{''}(x) > 0$$ for all $$(0,\infty)$$ , we conclude that $$x = \sqrt{300}$$ gives rise to the absolute minimum of $$f$$ . statement.paragraph: Inventory Control and Planning The demand for Super Titan tires is $$1,000,000 \slash {year}$$ . The setup cost for each production run is $$\$ 4000$$ , and the manufacturing cost is $${\$ 20} \slash {tire}$$ . The cost of storing each tire over the year is $$\$ 2$$ . Assuming uniformity of demand throughout the year and instantaneous production, determine how many tires should be manufactured per production run to keep the total cost to a minimum.

answer.paragraph: Let $$x$$ denote the number of tires in each production run. Then, the average number of tires in storage is $$x \slash 2$$ , so the storage cost incurred by the company is $$2(x \slash 2)$$ , or $$x$$ dollars. Next, since the company needs to manufacture $$1,000,000$$ tires for the year to meet the demand, the number of production runs is $$1,000,000 \slash x$$ . This gives setup costs amounting to
dollars for the year. The total manufacturing cost is $$\$ 20,000,000$$ . Thus, the total yearly cost incurred by the company is given by
Setting $$C^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ gives $$63,246$$ as the critical number in the interval $$(0,\ 1,000,000)$$ . Next, we find

Since $$C^{''}(x) > 0$$ for all $$x > 0$$ , we see that the graph of $$C$$ is concave upward for all $$x > 0$$ . Furthermore, $$C^{''}(63,246) > 0$$ implies that $$x = 63,246$$ gives rise to a relative minimum of $$C$$ (by the Second Derivative Test). Since the graph of $$C$$ is always concave upward for $$x > 0$$ , $$x = 63,246$$ gives the absolute minimum of $$C$$ . Therefore, the company should manufacture $$63,246$$ tires in each production run.

(Assume that each shipment of bottles is used up before the next shipment arrives.)

exercise_group.instructions: Fill in the blanks.

item.paragraph: A function $$f$$ is increasing on an interval $$I$$ if for any two numbers $$x_{1}$$ and $$x_{2}$$ in $$I$$ , $$x_{1} < x_{2}$$ implies that $$f\left( x_{1} \right) < f\left( x_{2} \right)$$ .
A function $$f$$ is decreasing on an interval $$I$$ if for any two numbers $$x_{1}$$ and $$x_{2}$$ in $$I$$ , $$x_{1} < x_{2}$$ implies that $$f\left( x_{1} \right) > f\left( x_{2} \right)$$ .
If $$f$$ is differentiable on an open interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ and $$f^{\prime}(x) > 0$$ on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ , then $$f$$ is increasing on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ .
If $$f$$ is differentiable on an open interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ and $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ , then $$f$$ is decreasing on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ .
If $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ for each value of $$x$$ in the interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ , then $$f$$ is constant on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ .
A function $$f$$ has a relative maximum at $$c$$ if there exists an open interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ containing $$c$$ such that $$f(x) \leq f(c)$$ for all $$x$$ in $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ .
A function $$f$$ has a relative minimum at $$c$$ if there exists an open interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ containing $$c$$ such that $$f(x) \geq f(c)$$ for all $$x$$ in $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ .
A critical number of a function $$f$$ is any number in the domain of $$f$$ at which $$f^{\prime}(c)$$ $$= 0$$ or $$f^{\prime}(c)$$ does not exist.
If $$f$$ has a relative extremum at $$c$$ , then $$c$$ must be a/an critical number of $$f$$ .
If $$c$$ is a critical number of $$f$$ , then $$f$$ may or may not have a/an relative extremum at $$c$$ .
The graph of a differentiable function $$f$$ is concave upward on an interval $$I$$ if $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ is increasing on $$I$$ .
If $$f$$ has a second derivative on an open interval $$I$$ and $$f^{''}(x)$$ $$> 0$$ on $$I$$ , then the graph of $$f$$ is concave upward on $$I$$ .
If the graph of a continuous function $$f$$ has a tangent line at $$P\left( {c,f(c)} \right)$$ and the graph of $$f$$ changes concavity at $$P$$ , then $$P$$ is called an inflection point of $$f$$ .

Suppose $$f$$ has a second derivative on an interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ , containing a critical number $$c$$ of $$f$$ . If $$f^{''}(c) < 0$$ , then $$f$$ has a/an relative maximum at $$c$$ . If $$f^{''}(c) = 0$$ , then $$f$$ may or may not have a/an relative extremum at $$c$$ .

statement.paragraph: The line $$x = a$$ is a vertical asymptote of the graph $$f$$ if at least one of the following is true: $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a^{+}}f(x) =$$ $$\pm \infty$$ or $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a^{-}}f(x) =$$ $$\pm \infty$$ .
For a rational function $$f(x) = \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}$$ , the line $$x = a$$ is a vertical asymptote of the graph of $$f$$ if $$Q(a) =$$ $$0$$ but $$P(a) \neq$$ $$0$$ .
The line $$y = b$$ is a horizontal asymptote of the graph of a function $$f$$ if either $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}f(x) =$$ $$b$$ or $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}f(x) =$$ $$b$$ .

item.paragraph: A function $$f$$ has an absolute maximum at $$c$$ if $$f(x) \leq f(c)$$ for all $$x$$ in the domain $$D$$ of $$f$$ . The number $$f(c)$$ is called the absolute maximum value of $$f$$ on $$D$$ .
A function $$f$$ has a relative minimum at $$c$$ if $$f(x) \geq f(c)$$ for all values of $$x$$ in some open interval containing $$c$$ .

statement.paragraph: The extreme value theorem states that if $$f$$ is continuous on the closed interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ , then $$f$$ has both a/an absolute maximum value and a/an absolute minimum value on $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ .

statement.paragraph: Find the interval(s) where $$f(x) = \frac{x^{2}}{1 - x}$$ is increasing and where it is decreasing.

answer.paragraph: Decreasing on $$\left( {- \infty,0} \right)$$ and $$\left( {2,\infty} \right)$$ ; increasing on $$\left( {0,1} \right)$$ and $$\left( {1,2} \right)$$

statement.paragraph: Find the relative maxima and relative minima, if any, of $$f(x) = 2x^{2} - 12x^{1 \slash 3}$$ .

Find the intervals where the graph of $$f(x) = \frac{1}{3}x^{3} - \frac{1}{4}x^{2} - \frac{1}{2}x + 1$$ is concave upward, the intervals where the graph of $$f$$ is concave downward, and the inflection point(s) of $$f$$ .

answer.paragraph: Concave downward on $$\left( {- \infty,\frac{1}{4}} \right)$$ ; concave upward on $$\left( {\frac{1}{4},\infty} \right)$$ ; $$\left( {\frac{1}{4},\frac{83}{96}} \right)$$

statement.paragraph: Sketch the graph of $$f(x) = 2x^{3} - 9x^{2} + 12x - 1$$ .

figure.alt_text: A curve is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The horizontal axis ranges from around negative 4 to beyond 6 and the vertical axis ranges from below 4 to over 10. The curve enters the third quadrant, very close to the vertical axis, slopes upward to the right, cuts the y axis at (0, negative 2), enters the fourth quadrant, cuts the horizontal axis very close to origin, enters the first quadrant, slopes upward to the right, concave down, reaches its high point at (1, 4), slopes downward to the right, after it inflects, concave up, then it reaches the low point at (2, 3) and continues to slope upward to the right, concave up.

statement.paragraph: Find the absolute maximum and absolute minimum values of $$f(x) = 2x^{3} + 3x^{2} - 1$$ on the interval $$\left\lbrack {- 2,3} \right\rbrack$$ .

answer.paragraph: Absolute minimum value: $$- 5$$ ; absolute maximum value: $$80$$

statement.paragraph: An open bucket in the form of a right circular cylinder is to be constructed with a capacity of $$1{ft}^{3}$$ . Find the radius and height of the cylinder if the amount of material used is minimal.
